title: Hanuman's reminder
hookLine: a new king forgets his promise, and the four aims of a life
carry: kama is a real aim, but dharma comes first

cards: Down in Kishkindha, the new king is having a wonderful time, and Valmiki doesn't hide it. Sugriva has his kingdom back after years on the run. He has his wife Ruma back, and Tara is in the palace as his queen as well.
He spends the season in comfort, feasting and drinking, with music in the halls. Up on the mountain, the rain falls on a cave. Then the rains end.
The sky clears. And Sugriva hasn't noticed.

teach.b: Hanuman notices. He goes to Sugriva first, before anyone gets angry. You have your kingdom, he says.
Now it's time to help your friends. Rama helped you; it's your turn. Sugriva hears him, and orders the monkey armies gathered from every mountain and forest within fifteen days.
Notice what Hanuman doesn't say. He doesn't tell Sugriva that enjoying himself was wicked, and Hindu teaching has a frame for why.
It names four aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, doing what's right; artha, wealth and security; kama, pleasure and love; and moksha, freedom. Kama is on the list.
Music, food, love, a festival: in Hindu teaching these are real goods, not sins to be ashamed of. What the tradition asks about is order.
Artha and kama are meant to be pursued inside dharma, not instead of it. As many teachers tell it, Sugriva's feast isn't the fault. The fault is that the feast pushed out a promise to a friend.
Hanuman doesn't take the music away. He puts dharma back on top.

Meanwhile the season turns. Autumn arrives, sharad: rivers clear, the sky is clean, the roads open. It's the season Hindus still fill with festivals, Navaratri's nine nights for the Goddess, full of dance, then Dussehra.

teach.h: KAMA IS REAL; DHARMA COMES FIRST.
teach.b: Joy and devotion in the same week. Up on Prasravana, Rama sees the clear sky and hears no word. And it meets a life now: a Hindu doesn't have to choose between fun and faith.
Dance at garba till midnight. Just keep your word in the morning.

how: Hindu teaching names four aims of life, the purusharthas: dharma, artha, kama and moksha. Autumn (sharad) opens the festival season, with Navaratri and Dussehra; in some regions Dussehra celebrates Rama's victory, in others Durga's.

o: the monsoon months that end in a clear autumn
the floods Hanuman crosses to reach Lanka
a drought that ends when Sugriva is crowned

games.q: the end of the rains — tap the pairs.
p: autumn, the season to set out
pleasure and love, a real aim of life

s: Sugriva remembers the search on his own
Hindu teaching counts pleasure as a sin
kama is one of the four aims of life, pursued inside dharma.
Hanuman speaks to Sugriva before anyone gets angry
he goes to him first, privately and carefully.

games.q: it's Navaratri: garba every night, and you promised to help your little cousin study this week. by the four aims, what fits?
o: skip garba; fun is a distraction from religion.
dance, and keep the promise: kama inside dharma.
dance every night; the promise can wait.
games.why: Hanuman didn't take Sugriva's music away. he put the promise back on top.

practice: Many Hindus offer food first, at the home shrine or silently, then eat it as prasad, a gift given back. Try it in the mind. Picture something you'll enjoy today: a meal, a song, time with a friend.
Breathe in and offer it. Breathe out and receive it back as a gift. If you don't pray, pause and thank whoever made it possible.

wordCard.voice: The rains. They end in a clear autumn sky, a feast that forgot a promise, and Hanuman's reminder.

orig.note: Sanskrit puruṣārtha: an aim of human life; traditionally four: dharma, artha, kama and moksha.

carryVoice: Your line: kama is a real aim, but dharma comes first. Enjoy the feast; keep the promise. That's day five hundred ninety.
